idiom_name: local functions capturing the enclosing method's variables
implementation_notes: C# 7 local functions do the job of the method object directly: every local variable and parameter of the containing member is accessible in a non-static local function, and writes to those captured variables are shared with the enclosing method, so a long method decomposes into named steps without any class (learn.microsoft.com). Since C# 8 a local function can be declared static when it captures nothing, which keeps it a plain private method and avoids the compiler-generated closure; capturing local functions may use a struct instead of a class for the closure, but only if the function is never converted to a delegate. Write the classic nested private class with fields when the algorithm must outlive the call, be tested directly or be reused - the closure is allocated per containing-method call.
pitfalls: A capturing local function makes the compiler allocate the closure (a display class, or a struct that is passed by reference): in hot paths prefer static local functions that take their state as parameters.
Converting a capturing local function to a delegate forces the heap allocation that direct calls can avoid, and the delegate keeps the captured variables alive afterwards.
Local functions may be referenced before their definition, but definite-assignment rules require every captured variable to be assigned before the call, not merely before the definition.
